results.title: Christmas cards or digital greetings? Ghanaians weigh in on festive tradition
results.content: The tradition of exchanging handwritten Christmas cards appears to be giving way to faster digital greetings, but some Ghanaians say physical cards still hold a special sentimental value. As social media and instant messaging platforms increasingly shape how people communicate, the annual exchange of Christmas cards has become less common for some. Yet, for others, receiving a handwritten card remains a meaningful expression of affection and goodwill. In a Joy FM vox pop, respondents shared their preferences, with some recalling childhood memories associated with Christmas cards while others pointed to the convenience of digital messages. Desmond Oware said he prefers receiving physical greeting cards because they remind him of how his parents used to decorate their home during Christmas.

results.title: Ghanaians share simple acts of kindness they plan to spread this Christmas
results.content: As the Christmas season approaches, some Ghanaians are looking beyond the usual festivities, identifying simple ways to make the season more meaningful for others. In a Joy FM vox pop, respondents shared plans to show kindness through gifts, food and other gestures aimed at making someone happy during the festive period. Raymond Asante said he intends to buy a live chicken for a friend as his way of spreading kindness. “One act of kindness that I want to do this Christmas is to buy a live chicken for my friend,” he said. Princess Appong also plans to brighten someone's Christmas by buying them a T-shirt. “One act of kindness I plan to do this Christmas is to buy someone a T-shirt,” she said.

results.title: One in three countries does not measure its air pollution, global report finds
results.content: One in every three countries in the world has no government system for measuring air pollution, leaving nearly one billion people without official information about the air they breathe, a new global report has found. The report, 2026 Open Air Quality Data: The Global Landscape, was released on 16 November by OpenAQ, a non-profit that runs the world’s largest open-source, open-access database of outdoor air quality measurements. It examined 198 countries, including the 193 UN member states. It found that 67 per cent of countries (two in every three) conduct or sponsor continuous air quality monitoring, up from 64 per cent in 2024. That leaves 65 countries with no evidence of government monitoring. Nearly one billion people live in them (roughly one in every eight people on Earth), and seven in 10 of those people live in low-income or lower-middle-income countries.

results.title: More than half of African countries do not measure their air pollution, report shows
results.content: More than half of Africa’s 54 countries have no government system for measuring air pollution, according to an analysis of a new global report, even as the continent leads the world in setting up new monitoring. The report, 2026 Open Air Quality Data: The Global Landscape, was released on 16 November by OpenAQ, a non-profit that runs the world’s largest open-source, open-access database of outdoor air quality measurements. It assessed whether governments in 198 countries measure their air quality and share the data with the public. An analysis of the report’s country-by-country data shows that 29 African countries have no evidence of government air quality monitoring. results.title: Eastern NDC youth organiser backs Opong-Fosu for National Chairmanship
results.content: The Eastern Regional Youth Organiser of the National Democratic Congress (NDC), Richard Etornam Nyarko, has declared his support for former Local Government Minister Dr Akwasi Opong-Fosu in the party’s National Chairmanship race. Mr Nyarko said the NDC, as a governing party, needed stable and experienced leadership to manage its national affairs and maintain cohesion. He made the remarks on Thursday, November 19, 2026, when Dr Opong-Fosu and his campaign team met regional executives in Koforidua to begin the Eastern Region leg of his campaign tour. Sharing his position on the contest, Mr Nyarko said: “A party in power doesn't need a chaotic leader.” He described Dr Opong-Fosu as “the right man for the job at this point in time”, citing the need for steady leadership within the party.
